Man, was I hyped to try this game for the first time. It seemed like everything I'd wanted from a game. Post-apocalyptic atmosphere, massive open world, world-building through 'show, don't tell,' and sandbox gameplay.

But, uh, this game feels like it was made by a guy with Asperger's syndrome who wanted to make a game for purely himself to enjoy because he couldn't get over his social anxiety to go out and interact in the real world. What I mean by that, is this game just doesn't play like an actual game. It plays like what someone would want if they never wanted to actually live in real life. It's, kiiiiinda a simulation sandbox? There's fun, quirky AI to play with. That's it. No physics, no puzzles, literally ♥♥♥♥ all. Nothing you do in the game has any cause and affect. It's like a wet dream for people with pattern recognition. 

This game, like many other things in this modern world, is a shining example of what I find to be a phenomena where people seem to worship certain media entities, for no particular reason. This game is not even a game. There is no purpose, no reason, no beginning, no end. Minecraft was a sandbox, but also gave me a reason to play it lmao. You could create things, exploit things, imagine things.

This game is a 10/10 ass cheeks and I think the developer is just micro-dosing mushrooms every day, and the people giving this game overwhelmingly positive reviews are either meme'ing, coping, or having a giant beard underneath their neck with nothing illuminating their faces but the cold blue tint of their OLED monitors glaring at 100% brightness from their mothers basement.

For example, my frist few playthroughs were just surviving and getting by with a small gang trying to evade wildlife and slavers while looking for a safe place to setup a small base and a farm. The funny thing is I eventually figured out is that there is no safe place in the world of kenshi, when picking a location for a base the game forces you to consider which threats you are willing/can deal with and which you would rather avoid or cannot deal with. Playing as an adventurer / trader solo or with a small group without a base completely changes the gameplay as you will need to approach the game differently and will face different challanges and threats while traveling.

Fast forward to current playthorugh, I am waging war on one of the major factions, harrasing their patrols, inflitrating their cities, stealing tech and valuables, and kidnapping leaders and nobles to  destabilize their cities. The captives I then offer to their enemy (Shek & Skeletons) and that way I am forming alliances to form combined attacks and takeovers of their cities, one by one, untill the faction is completely shattered and no longer a threat. And after that its on to the next faction.

In case you are wondering, my campaign list is the Holy Nation > Smaller slaver factions and the slave market > the United Cities and the Traders Guild > Cannibals, bandits, hostile hive's, fogmen, thralls, and eventually march a massive army to crush CatLon and whatever is left of his empire.

Then there is the workshop with mods ranging from simple content additions to mods that completely overhaul the game, mechanics, combat, factions, and more lore. There are DLC quality and content level overhauls like Genesis for example!

While the game can be fun for a short period, I was surprised with how incomplete many systems are, especially given the age and the reputation of this game. In short, I would suggest waiting for the sequel, as it seems likely there is no chance existing mechanics are improved. 

I could give numerous examples, but to start: the faction mechanics are almost impossible to interact with, bar extreme world changing events like killing a faction leader. There are no familiar quest systems or low-level bounties to improve your standing with a faction. Like most things with Kenshi, an online search will suggest an exploit or mod to get around this. Another example is the shop counter, which should allow you to manage your own store, but is bugged due to a broken NPC wage system. 

NPC interactions are extremely limited and the world feels rather lifeless. There are lots of people walking about, sure, but you can't talk to most of them, and those you can are usually unnamed shopkeepers with generic dialogue. There are entire major cities without any non-generic interactable NPCs. 

While combat is visually pleasing at times, there's a strange restriction wherein you can't kill downed enemies. So you can chop off limbs by chance, but if someone is knocked out, you have to wait for them to stand up to hit them again.

As far as RPGs go, Kenshi’s versatility is nearly unmatched. It feels less like a game built around one genre and more like a game that keeps absorbing the best ideas from others.

Love isometric RPGs like Wasteland or Pillars of Eternity? Kenshi gives you the freedom, systems and party management you’d expect, but drops you into a world that refuses to revolve around your story. Prefer colony sims like RimWorld or Stranded: Alien Dawn? You’ll find similarly deep mechanics, except your colony exists within a much larger, more dangerous and politically complicated world. Enjoy the environmental storytelling of Elden Ring? Kenshi tells its story through ruins, scars, factions and the things you discover when you wander somewhere you were never meant to survive.

There’s a satisfying grind and progression system reminiscent of RuneScape, minus the shackles of an MMO. There’s a dynamic trade economy, faction politics, base-building, slavery, warfare, exploration and even faction creation. And if you want multiplayer, there’s apparently a mod for that, too.

You get the point: Kenshi is extraordinarily versatile. It can become the game you want it to be.

But that flexibility comes at a cost.

Kenshi does not hold your hand. Not even a little.

You’ll be confused. You’ll be directionless. You’ll get beaten half to death by starving bandits, enslaved, robbed, eaten or otherwise reminded that you are not the protagonist of this world. When you begin, you’re so weak and unequipped that even surviving can feel like an accomplishment. I wouldn’t blame anyone for falling off within the first hour.

That initial frustration is the barrier. It is also the point.

Because Kenshi isn’t interested in giving you a heroic journey. It gives you a starting condition: a nobody with no money, no power and no guarantee that tomorrow will be better than today. Your story only begins once you figure out how to survive long enough to write it.

Eventually, the confusion starts to give way to understanding. The beating becomes training. The poverty becomes motivation. The aimlessness becomes freedom. You stop waiting for the game to tell you what to do and start creating your own reasons to keep going.

That’s when Kenshi becomes something genuinely special.

It is a one-of-a-kind experience, and one of the few games that can permanently change how you think about role-playing games. Once you’ve watched a nobody crawl out of the dirt, build a crew, establish a home and become powerful enough to reshape the world around them, it becomes difficult to look at other games the same way.

Be patient with Kenshi. It may not welcome you warmly, but if you stick with it, it will give you something few games can: a story that feels entirely, unmistakably yours.

Come, sit by the fire and let me tell you a story. 

A day where I stumbled upon a funny map in a game where someone was looking to build a base location. A map that meant little to me and was quickly forgotten, but was just enough of a sting that it brought me to look and try the game. 

I started a standard run in the hub, learned of the shops and things I might buy. Then boldly ran into this great unknown world, landing upon a ruined settlement and making a save as I scavenged the ruins for all it had. Intending to make my way back to the hub to sell my new goods, I was met with cute little dogs who quickly mauled me. I reloaded my save. 

What followed was probably a few hours of me doing my best to sneak back and forth until I was satisfied to have sold everything. And making my way in a new direction into a city run by boney humanoid people. Where I got my first companion. But before she and I set out too far, we quickly found a wandering trader who we bought a cute baby bull off of who I promptly named Bullseye. In spite of being a child, this little guy quickly showed that they were the best of us as they almost singlehandedly defeated a group of bandits, saving Ruka and I. 

With this small start of a squad, I remembered the map that brought me here. And a distant land labeled: "friendly humans" in the far south east. A place, I thought, where maybe I could build a home away from constant save scumming of every early battle. 

And so we set off on one of the greatest pilgrimages a game has ever taken me through. 
Sneaking through swamps, past hoards alien spiders in a land completely different to the one I had started my journey in. A few hours later, I found myself in civilization; a city called Mourn in a place called the bonefields. A place I thought appropriate as I saw hoards of dogs. But it is here, that I  restocked, and met my 3rd companion on our journey east. Adopting a pet puppy of my own along not too long after.

Blissfully unaware, I saw how much distance we had traveled and just how close we were to my promised land, and knew that before long, I would have a home. 

What followed, was the longest part of the journey, where I continued to only barely survive, saving and reloading as needed. Allowing enemies I found to battle one another and take in the spoils of their battle for myself. 

I learned quickly of giant beasts, and a seeming kingdom of alien humanoids. A territory of which I tried to remain on the outskirts of.
Finding myself eventually, so close to my goal, in a abandoned town, where I hid inside and learned I could fire upon the giant beasts from relative safety and recover my barely surviving team.  

Recovered, we set out one final time, as we attempted and repeatedly failed to make our way into this sacred valley of my dreams. The way was blocked by seeming small armies of hostiles, upon a hill flanked by two plateaus. If this had been the lord of the rings journey, this was my black gate. Nearly impossible seeming for my band to sneak through. 

But like most of the journey, after repeated attempts, we made it. We made it through this black gate to a land that brought me even more visions of lotr and the lands of mordor. But we had made it. And I was determined to find this human civilization. "Maybe this is a place where the harsh landscape has brought people together. I'd like to be part of that." I was ready to join this band. 

Oh, my fellow traveler, I found my friendly humans. I did. And that was just the beginning. In a game that once I opened, I found hard to put down. And one I still have not fully explored. 

If you seek the journey, you will learn well my advice, that though you may lose much, the skin on your back is the most precious commodity.

Kenshi is an amazing open world game that really managed to sink its claws into me. All the choices are in the palm of your hand as you are fully free to focus on a chill/base building experience, go full murder/combat, explore and everywhere in between. You can further change the experience with the advanced settings, whether you want the game to be even more harsh than it can be or if you want it to be more chill. In either case the choice is fully yours. 

I have had plenty of memorable moments both when I was playing with just my MC and when I finally got around to recruiting people both for combat and for building a base. The game runs smooth like butter even at 4K and with visual mods. Speaking of mods you can further enhance the experience with the amazing visual, performance enhancing & QoL mods the community has created over the years. Feel free to look through my mod list if you want some ideas of what you can add to the game.

Overall between the base game and what the community has built, Kenshi is an amazing open world sandbox game that I think anyone interested in these styles of games should give a try. The game might kick your ass but you will have a grand time whether you are getting yours handed to you, doing the handing, just exploring or building a base. Kenshi will surely have something you can do that appeals to your style of gameplay in an open world game.

There’s really nothing else quite like it. Starting with a handful of useless nobodies and eventually building a powerful squad, a functioning base, and enough confidence to fight entire factions is incredibly satisfying. The freedom to play however you want is easily the game’s biggest strength, although the late game can feel a little empty once your squad is strong, your research is mostly complete, and you’ve run out of meaningful goals to chase.

That said, Kenshi is held together with duct tape and hope. The bugs can be frustrating, the pathfinding regularly makes terrible decisions, and managing a large squad sometimes feels like supervising a field trip where everyone is actively trying to get lost.

Mods also feel almost required for the best experience. Quality-of-life improvements, world-state mods, UI changes, and bug fixes smooth out a lot of rough edges that probably should have been handled by the base game.

Kenshi is clunky, ugly, confusing, and occasionally infuriating, but it is also genuinely unique and very hard to put down once it clicks.

Kenshi is a surprisingly deep and engaging game. Great progression that's individual for every character, (although brutally difficult in the beginning), a dauntingly huge map with an absurdly huge amount of choices for where to go.

I do however have 2 negatives to bring up. With the Sci-Fi setting not having any kind of firearms is a hugely missed opportunity and feels like they should be there, but it's missing. And for new players there's a lack of direction and tutorial in my opinion. You're thrown into the world and get a figurative pat on the back and a "You're out here now, good luck!".

Some more explained details on the world, the in game mechanics and a more interactive tutorial wouldn't go amiss. But besides these 2 things I don't really have any complaints about it, except that I would personally like if the dialogue was voice acted. It does what it's supposed to incredibly well, the mod support is amazing with many fun additions you can throw into the game quite easily.

I was a bit sceptical at first since the gameplay looked more action oriented than it is, and the game doesn't have controller support. But a good way to describe the controls is Kotor, but with less combat options, base building and a larger party system.

Overall I give Kenshi 8.5/10. If guns (natively, not through mods), a longer and interactive tutorial, and voice acting are added it'll easily become a full 10/10!

# Kenshi — A Review

**Developer:** Lo-Fi Games | **Genre:** Open-World Sandbox RPG | **Platform:** PC

---

There is a moment early in Kenshi — maybe your third or fourth hour in — where you realize the game is never going to hold your hand. Your character has just been beaten unconscious by a wandering band of bandits, left bleeding in the dirt of a sun-scorched wasteland, with no quest marker telling you where to go and no tutorial pop-up offering consolation. And somehow, impossibly, you can't wait to get back up.

Kenshi is not a game of questlines. It's a game of emergent stories — of being a shopkeeper and a thief, a lone wanderer and a slave, and eventually an entire community of people working together to one day erect a city in the wasteland. The game never scripted any of it. It just gave you a world and stepped back.

At its core, Kenshi is an open-world RPG with real-time strategy elements and no linear narrative, set in a post-apocalyptic world where survival is brutally difficult. You begin with no skills and struggle simply to stay alive, leveling up abilities through use — thievery by stealing, combat by fighting — and slowly recruiting others to grow your band.

Eventually it becomes a surprisingly effective management game as you research technologies, construct buildings, and assign your people long lists of automated tasks — mining, farming, construction. The scope of what you can build toward is staggering. The path to get there is unforgiving.

That difficulty is the game's defining trait and its biggest barrier. The concept of a free-roaming RPG where you craft your own story is always intriguing, and the world is vast and impressive for a small indie project, but the game does a poor job of communicating its intricate systems to new players. There is no onboarding. You are expected to fail, learn, and try again. Whether that sounds like a feature or a flaw will determine whether Kenshi is for you.

At first glance it looks like a psychotic, twisted experiment. The graphics engine barely holds itself together under its many systems. There are bugs, rough optimization, and slow loading times. Visually, it will never win awards. The mechanics, however, are tremendous and extremely detailed — clearly a labor of love deserving of high praise.

What makes Kenshi genuinely special is its atmosphere. The world feels ancient, indifferent, and alive in ways most games can't replicate. Factions have their own ideologies and agendas. Cities feel lived-in. Every biome — from scorched flats to swamp-laden coastlines — carries a distinct personality. The world is fascinating, the myriad of ways to approach and play it enormous, and for those it grabs, it could easily consume all of your free time.

By May 2026, the game had sold 3 million copies — a remarkable achievement for a small studio with a niche, demanding product. Word of mouth and Steam reviews have kept it alive for years, and a dedicated modding community has only deepened the experience.

Kenshi is not a game for everyone. It is slow, obtuse, rough around every edge, and asks a great deal of patience before it gives anything back. But for those willing to meet it on its own terms, it offers something rare: a world that generates genuine legend. Your stories won't come from a writer. They'll come from the dust, the violence, and the unlikely triumphs you carved out yourself.

**Verdict: 8/10** — A singular, deeply flawed masterpiece of emergent storytelling. Brutal, beautiful, and completely unlike anything else.

1st gripe:
If you're planning to play this game with a controller(or on a steam deck in my case), don't bother. All the tutorials and help this game gives you all assume you're playing on a keyboard. I'm no stranger to weird and clunky controls clearly meant for a keyboard and haphazardly being mapped to a controller, but this one just takes the cake. If you're forced to play on a controller on this game, you're basically screwed. Even moreso than the people who play this game on their pc. 

2nd gripe:
The game is very unintuitive. Now I've played some hella unintuitive games before(funger & funger 2, coe 5, and rimworld), but this one just takes it to a whole nother level that is frankly unfun.

When I try to form up a squad(like the tutorial blurb told me to), I get shot with a 6K price tag from john gunsmith. When I finally stumble unto the merchant after looking at a barren dessert and 30 minutes of fighting with the controls, the funds that I started as a wanderer may as well have been 0. When I try to build a small shack(cuz that's what the very first tutorial blurb i read outside of the pc controls ones said I needed to do to build a research bench), I get hit with "it's too close to a town", "this building needs 15K", and when I manage to find a spot it required 5 building materials that cost an arm and a leg outside where there's literally nothing. 

All this work just to access the very first concept the game taught me which was a research bench. I am sure it's better on pc, but labelling this game as "playable" on the steam deck oled is just false.

In conclusion, I really did want to give this game a chance. The community around it has made some amazing content and has told some amazing stories with it. But as a game, it has fallen short for me. I hope Kenshi 2 provides a better experience than this.

Ah, Kenshi.  I purchased this game after watching numerous Youtube videos of people doing their own creative / fun "runs" (such as a slave to business owner run, or a farming run, etc).  Each looked pretty neat, and as an avid Rimworld fan I thought "Hey, this is sort of like Rimworld but in third person 3d!".  Next steam sale, I excitedly hit purchase.

Well, I stand here now having installed the game and tried it for myself, and... "underwhelmed" doesn't do it justice.  Have you ever played really old MMO's, like EverQuest or DAOC?  Imagine hopping back in now, same graphics and all, and there was no tutorial or training missions to at least familiarize yourself with the controls.  Great, I did it to myself again, I purchased yet another game where I'm expected to watch hours of Youtube videos for stuff that the game itself refuses to teach.

There seems like there's potential here, if you want a super sandboxy open world type thing where there isn't any sort of story, plot, or world events.  It does seem to be one of those "Everything and the kitchen sink, too" sort of games, where if you have an idea - you can accomplish it.  I'm just typically not that creative, and need at least SOME degree of direction  to start playing a game. 

I may revise my review in the future if I give it another try, but I fear that this may be one of those games that's going to be more interesting to watch other people play, than to actually play myself.  Maybe I'm missing something, but my brain was practically SCREAMING at me, "Now what?".

**Update with more detail**
Gave it one more quick shot since I'm a bit of a masochist / hate wasting money on something I just purchased.  I genuinely feel like I'm missing something crucial to having fun here, because both times I got dropped into the "Wanderer" start - I felt like a toddler who was abandoned in the middle of an airport; confused, lost, directionless, and perhaps a bit scared.  After wandering aimlessly around the starting area for a while, I finally had enough and uninstalled this thing.  Main issues were:

**UI / Graphics**
I am not usually against "deep, impenetrable" UI's - hell, one of my favorite games is the X-series of space games, which is perhaps the most menu driven game I've ever played.  Likewise, graphics aren't usually all that important to me, with Rimworld being my favorite game.  Despite this somehow though, Kenshi's UI is downright horrid and clunky, with buttons scattered all over the screen that go completely unexplained.  The graphics itself don't do it any justice either, with animations and models looking like something out of a circa ~2000 game (Deus Ex 1, etc).

The game very much could do with a UI overhaul, and perhaps a graphics overhaul mod as well.  Do these exist?

**Gameplay / Plot**
Biggest issue right here  - having watched folks online play this game, the thought never occurred to me that this would be a total grind-fest in order to accomplish anything.  Skills take hours and hours to level up to a level that would be considered usable, your character is utterly useless at the beginning and will fold like a cheap piece of origami.  Folks love to say that this is the point, and you "need to embrace losing" - but to be frank, that isn't really fun.  It's tedious.  I hate the whole "Losing is Fun" mentality from the Dwarf Fortress fandom, it's no different here.

Add in the fact that there's no quests, no direction, not even a vague sense of plot to really dig into.  The question I keep asking myself is "Why am I doing this?  What is the point?".  If I free all the slaves (where are they, how do I find them, who knows!), it doesn't seem to make any difference to the world, and doesn't net you any rewards.  Likewise if I make a outpost in the middle of the desert, it just feels so... aimless.  Like being the only person playing an MMO that everyone else stopped playing 10 years ago.  Perhaps there's mods out there that let me start as a "pre-built" character with combat abilities already existing, but it still begs the question of 'for what purpose?".

**Over-reliance on external material / time investment*
Posts often refer people to watch various "newbie" youtube videos, or read guides in order to properly start this game without feeling totally lost.  Some may like this, but this is a telltale sign of poor game design if you ask me; I shouldn't have to quit the game to watch an hour+ of someone explaining basic mechanics - that's what tutorials and newbie zones are for.  Please don't force me to do 'homework' just because the devs are too lazy to put in tutorials (and yes, for a 1.0 release, it's pretty damn unexcuseable).

Likewise I frequently hear "Oh, you only played 3 hours, you really need to play at least 20 to truly have it click", and again - that doesn't exactly sound like good game design.  This sounds more like Stockholm Syndrome for video games, if something isn't enjoyable for the first hour, I'm not going to waste my time.  I also loathe the fact that so many people compared this game to Rimworld, since it's pretty much NOTHING alike.  I'd say it's closer to a Project Zomboid, but with a heck of a lot more bugs and a truly atrocious UI.

**Conclusion**
Kenshi checks a lot of the boxes I love in survival / third person games - a supposedly decent crafting system, the ability to colonize anywhere, build bases, etc.  That said, this is exactly why it's so disappointing that I found it so devoid of life, bland, an absolute chore to play, and a complete grindfest.  Maybe some folks can suggest mods that fix a lot of my gripes, maybe they're "unfixable" and the problem is that I simply lack the ability to play "100% sandbox" games.  

All in all, I don't think this is for me.  This feels like an early access game that had development abandoned halfway through, they slapped a 1.0 on it and called it done.

 I'd recommend this game to MMO players, Colony Builder players, and Survival Game players looking for a decent single player RPG. I've played a decent amount of both sandbox MMO's and Theme Park ones. There's a lot of differences between MMORPG's and single player RPG's. (especially the sand box type. Theme park  MMO's typically set the players up in that OP way now). One of those differences is the idea that you are simply a cog in the machine, and the NPC's also have this applied. In pretty much 90% of RPG's set the player up into an OP mind set as the game continues. Which is fine, but it's incredibly predictable and boring and I personally always preferred a sandbox RPG. But it was a game type mostly held by MMO's at the time like Ultima Online, SWG, OSRS (to a certain degree.), DaoC and more recently Albion online. We also saw this type of game evolve into the sandbox games we see today like Rust and DayZ. 

But this is one of those games where you lose track of the time while building your base or collecting resources or simply just exploring and fighting the many types of enemies found through out the world. I heard someone say at one point "It's Fallot NV but with Katanas." Which I don't think does it justice.

It's a sandbox through and through. And in a sandbox, that group of lads 2 years older than you, that might just decide to come and kick over your sandcastle. The game doesn't care if you survive, it doesn't care what you're doing currently. Things and elements simply happen and you have to work around that as a player, and that's where the story of Kenshi typically lies. 

The closest games that resemble this game would be games like Rimworld, ONI, Cosmoteer, Factorio, Dwarf Fortress and a few others I haven't played. However, those games are typically heavily reliant on an extensive gameplay loop that goes far deeper than in and sort of locks you to your base as you continue to upgrade and change each piece. Kenshi. In-game, you only need worry about 2 things. How much food you have and how much healing items you have (Maybe carry some artificial limbs because body parts can be cut off.) Simple, but effective gameplay elements that can be easily managed in various ways and methods within Kenshi, freeing you up to explore a vast open world. A brutal open world, but a vast one nonetheless. Hire some bodyguards to defend your base, then go exploring. The game opens up to you if you're willing to try your luck in travelling the dangerous and hazardous wastes. Your base is simply a safe point or a town NPC's can visit, as well as a place to heal up research and farm resources and get cats (Money.) The upgrades to get a fully upgraded wall and other base features is not much work. The game clearly is pushing you to explore instead of building over and over again.

Tips for people starting:
This game is very moddable with workshop content. However try not to import your game over and over when adding new mods because it can bug out. (My jobs broke on one play through and no one would perform tasks anymore.) So be careful, and start the game with the mods you want on there already. (My favourites are usually mods that add things to the game or apply different starts, the tech hunter start is a great beginner friendly start in Kenshi, as you spawn in a big town with copper and iron not too far away and in pretty amazing spot on top of a mountain.  You also start with really good gear, 5 pawns. So you only need to focus on combat to "really" make them stronger.

Find iron vein.
Find copper vein.
Put storage boxes for iron and copper.
recruit pawns from bars in towns, put them to work.
Make training dummies, put pawns on them to raise their combat.
Sell iron.
Make building materials by putting a stone mine down and a station to convert them to building material.
Make wheat, turn it into bread.
When you've built your base in or around the copper and iron veins, start making iron plates.
Sell Iron plates you don't need.
Go for combat always, getting attacked raises your pawns defence. Just don't die.

Even though it's buggy. It's a great game that I always seem to come back to, it gets me in terms of what I always wanted in a single player RPG. You're no hero, no OP cringe, And the world you traverse really does reflect that philosophy. Your objective is to survive, everything else is just a side mission. 

Great game that everyone who likes colony builders, brutal difficulty, Sandbox MMO's and survival games should be playing Kenshi to some degree.
